text: I’ll model the water as the Boolean union of the central 16 mm-radius sphere and six face-normal cylindrical passages, clipped by the 40 mm cube, then subtract the free 15 mm ball. This preserves the 1 mm spherical gap and yields 14 named boundaries: ball, hollow wall, six cylindrical hole walls, and six planar openings. I’ll first build and inspect the exact CAD at metre scale; the eventual volume mesh will use tetrahedra with local sizing fine enough to resolve the 1 mm gap.

The Boolean is a single connected water volume, but its 12 CAD faces indicate that some nominal boundaries are analytically continuous across Boolean intersections. I’ll inspect each face’s exact surface type, area, centre, and normal samples before assigning names; this avoids guessing patch identity from a bounding box.

The inspection exposed a construction error before export: transform composition rotated translations as well as cylinder axes, so the passages do not occupy the intended ±20 mm face locations. I’ll correct the model using cylinders defined directly by start point and axis direction, then verify the full extents and face taxonomy again.

`Cylinder` does not accept a workplane as its positional argument in this installed API. I’ll use the kernel-level cylinder constructor, which explicitly accepts a plane and therefore guarantees each global axis and start point.

The corrected cylinder axes now reveal the cube itself was shifted: this API’s `Box` is centred by default, so my additional −20 mm translation made it span −40 to 0 mm. I’ll remove that translation and rebuild; the required fluid must then span exactly ±20 mm and expose all six openings.

The rebuilt water has the correct ±20 mm extents, one solid, six planar openings, six cylindrical wall faces, eight spherical hollow-wall fragments, and one spherical ball face. I’ll now render the coarse tessellation and inspect each cylindrical face’s analytic rotation axis so the six hole-wall names come from the created passage directions rather than spatial heuristics.

The analytic axes confirm two wall faces per global axis; the sign of each face’s axial centre distinguishes its corresponding opening. The first render attempt failed only because this OSMesa build does not provide `start_xvfb`; I’ll render directly off-screen and retain the successful inspection step in the build script.

The preview matches the intended six-way flooded cage and visibly resolves the inner ball and surrounding shell. I’ll now form the 14 face sets from exact analytic surface classes, axis directions, and axial side; verify the requested radii from those surfaces and each opening area against \(\pi(12\,\mathrm{mm})^2\); then export all patches together so shared STL seams are welded.

I’ll export at 0.125 mm chord tolerance, one quarter of the intended 0.5 mm coarse near-wall cell and fine enough for the final refinement. The patch classifier uses only analytic geometry and authored axes; `hollowWall` collects the eight Boolean-fragmented pieces of the original 16 mm sphere.

The exported union is watertight and consistently wound (16,616 triangles, zero open/flipped/non-manifold edges). For the coarse mesh I’ll use a 1 mm Cartesian background over a 42 mm cube and one surface-refinement level, giving nominal 0.5 mm boundary cells—two cells across the minimum gap. The retained point is in the +z passage at `(0,0,18 mm)`, safely inside the connected water and outside the ball.
The coarse background mesh is correct: 74,088 cubic cells at exactly 1 mm. I’ll now castellate and snap it to the welded 14-patch surface, retaining only the connected water region.

`snappyHexMesh` stopped before meshing because this OpenFOAM release requires placeholder discretisation dictionaries even for mesh-only cases. I’ll add minimal mesh-case dictionaries and rerun; no solver fields or boundary conditions are being introduced.

Castellation successfully found the connected water region and produced 91,608 coarse cells, but snapping stopped because the installed quality template omits a scalar this snappy version expects. I’ll explicitly add `errorReduction`, regenerate the clean background mesh, and rerun snapping.

The next missing template entry is `nSmoothScale`, again a packaging mismatch rather than a geometry failure. I’ll inspect the installed quality dictionary once and explicitly supply any legacy snap parameters it lacks before another clean rerun.

The installed template indeed lacks both snap-iteration controls. I’ll add the standard `nSmoothScale 4`, keep `errorReduction 0.75`, and provide the conventional relaxed non-orthogonality limit, then rerun from the 1 mm background.

The coarse snapped mesh completed with 91,608 cells and no snappy quality violations. I’ll run the binding `checkMesh` now and inspect the resulting patch inventory and gap resolution before deciding whether the coarse two-cell gap needs one further refinement level.

The coarse mesh passes `checkMesh`, contains all 14 requested patches, and its volume (20.598 mL) is within 0.3% of the exact CAD volume (20.659 mL). I’ll render the mesh boundary and a central slice to visually confirm connectivity and the narrow shell before increasing surface refinement to four cells across the 1 mm gap.

The mesh converted cleanly to VTK. I’ll display the transparent boundary with a mid-plane cell slice; this specifically checks that the ball is excluded, the annular water layer remains connected, and the six passages meet the shell.

The central slice confirms the excluded ball, continuous annular shell, and open passages. Two cells across a 1 mm clearance is only a coarse topology check, so I’ll make the final mesh with refinement level 2 (nominal 0.25 mm boundary cells, approximately four cells across the minimum gap) while retaining the same exact patch surfaces and background extent.
The final refinement is still running beyond the initial execution window; I’ll wait for this existing mesher process rather than queueing another command.

The final mesh completed successfully with 433,122 cells, including 348,362 level-2 cells at nominal 0.25 mm near surfaces. I’ll now run the binding final `checkMesh`, confirm all 14 patches survived, and compare mesh volume to the exact CAD water volume.

Final validation: `checkMesh` reports **Mesh OK**, one connected region, 433,122 cells, 14 boundary patches, maximum non-orthogonality 49.6°, maximum skewness 1.96, and positive cell volumes. The mesh volume is 20.6695 mL versus 20.6585 mL exact CAD volume (0.053% difference).

Measured against the request:
- Cube extent: 40 mm, centred at the origin.
- Hollow support radius: 16.000 mm.
- Ball radius: 15.000 mm.
- Minimum spherical water gap: 1.000 mm.
- Six opening equivalent radii: 12.000 mm each.
- Final nominal near-surface cell size: 0.25 mm, about four cells through the minimum gap.
- All 14 patches are present, with one STL per patch in `constant/triSurface`.

No requested property was left unchecked. The only meshing choices not specified by the request were the 42 mm temporary background box, 1 mm base cells, 0.25 mm final surface cells, 0.125 mm STL chord tolerance, and the retained point `(0, 0, 18 mm)`; the background is removed from the final water mesh.

The completion gate correctly noted that the retained point was present in `snappyHexMeshDict` but absent from the STL manifest. I’ll re-export the identical welded patch set with `(0,0,18 mm)` recorded in `patches.json`; this does not alter the already validated geometry or mesh.
The surface manifest now records the same validated in-water point used by snappyHexMesh. All geometry, closure, patch, scale, and mesh checks are ready for final completion.
